lessons.title: The CIA triad
lessons.body: Confidentiality - only authorised people can read it. Integrity - it is not changed without permission. Availability - it works when needed. For any threat, ask which of the three it attacks.

lessons.title: AuthN vs AuthZ
lessons.body: Authentication = proving who you are. Authorisation = what you may do once known. Factors: something you know (password), have (key/phone), are (biometric). MFA mixes DIFFERENT factor types; two passwords is not MFA. Phishing-resistant MFA (passkeys, hardware keys) beats SMS codes.

lessons.title: Design rules
lessons.body: Least privilege - minimum access needed. Defense in depth - layer controls. Fail securely - deny on error. Zero trust - verify every request, never trust by location. Kerckhoffs: assume the attacker knows your design; only the keys are secret.

lessons.title: Hashing vs encryption
lessons.body: Encryption is reversible with a key (symmetric AES for bulk; asymmetric RSA/ECC for key exchange and signatures). Hashing is one-way, fixed-size output. Store passwords with a slow salted hash (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2) - never plain SHA-256, MD5, or reversible encryption. TLS uses asymmetric to agree a key, then symmetric for speed.

lessons.title: Attack classes and defenses
lessons.body: Phishing -> training, phishing-resistant MFA. SQL injection -> parameterised queries. XSS -> output encoding, CSP. Memory corruption -> memory-safe languages. MITM -> TLS with cert validation. DDoS -> rate limiting, CDNs. The pattern: most attacks exploit the line between DATA and CODE, or between trusted and untrusted input.

lessons.title: Rules of engagement
lessons.body: Only test systems you own or have WRITTEN permission to test. Unauthorised access is a crime (US CFAA, UK Computer Misuse Act). Practise legally: your own VM lab, deliberately vulnerable apps (OWASP Juice Shop, DVWA), and CTFs (picoCTF, TryHackMe, Hack The Box). Found a real bug? Use responsible disclosure or a bug bounty.

quiz.q: A DDoS attack mainly targets which CIA property?
quiz.why: It knocks a service offline: availability.
Know + have are different factor types.
Slow salted hashes make stolen databases expensive to crack.
Parameterised queries keep user input as data, never code.

quiz.q: Giving a program only the access it needs is...
quiz.why: Least privilege limits blast radius if it's compromised.
